lesson.title: The Register Ladder
lesson.subtitle: want→desire (desear), go in→enter (entrar), finish→terminate (terminar): formal English revealing everyday Spanish

hook.title: Your Fancy English Is Everyday Spanish
hook.content: Language Transfer's signature insight is the Register Ladder. In English, you have two ways to say almost everything: a casual Germanic phrase ('go in', 'keep on', 'finish', 'want') and a formal Latinate word ('enter', 'continue', 'terminate', 'desire'). What sounds stiff or formal in English is completely natural, everyday street Spanish: entrar ('to go in'), continuar ('to keep going'), terminar ('to finish'), desear ('to wish/want')!

footnotes.title: Why 'Terminate' Is Cozy in Spanish
footnotes.content: In English, Latin words arrived through royal courts, law, and science, so 'terminate' feels cold and technical. In Spain, Latin was the language of the kitchen and the playground — so terminar is simply 'to finish'!

pattern.title: Stepping Up in English to Step Across into Spanish
pattern.content: Whenever you get stuck looking for a Spanish word, don't reach for a dictionary — step one rung up the English register ladder! Trade 'finish' for 'terminate' and you have terminar. Trade 'go in' for 'enter' and you have entrar. And adjectives ending in -ante, -ente, or -ble (importante, diferente, posible, imposible) cross over with one s and no gender change!
pattern.trap_note: In Spanish, subject 'it' is invisible! For 'It is important' or 'It is possible', say Es importante / Es posible — never *Lo es importante.

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: entrar, terminar, desear, continuar, importante, posible
exercises.meaning: to go in (enter), to finish (terminate), to wish / desire, to keep going (continue), important, possible
exercises.explanation: Climbing from phrasal English to Latinate English hands you the everyday Spanish word.

exercises.prompt: Select every English sentence that expresses the same thought as 'Quiero terminar y entrar aquí':
exercises.meaning: I want to finish and go in here
renderings: I want to finish and go in here
I want to complete it and enter here
traps: I finished and went out from here
You want to start and wait there
exercises.target_answer: I want to finish and go in here
exercises.explanation: terminar covers both casual 'finish' and formal 'complete/terminate'; entrar covers both 'go in' and 'enter'!

exercises.prompt: Climb the register ladder from 'finish' to 'terminate' to write the Spanish infinitive:

exercises.explanation: Quiero + terminar — no 'to' needed between quiero and the infinitive.

exercises.idea: say that it is very important
exercises.explanation: Es muy importante — Spanish drops subject 'it' because es already carries it.

diagnosis.cue: Never use lo as a subject 'it' before es! Es alone means 'It is'.

summary.outcome: Use the English register ladder to unlock entrar, terminar, desear, continuar, importante, and posible.

use_example.german: Quiero terminar porque es muy importante.
use_example.english: I want to finish because it is very important.

summary.takeaway: When a casual English word hides the Spanish root, trade it for its formal Latinate synonym.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([2] The -CIÓN Bridge): unlock over a thousand feminine Spanish nouns with a single suffix.

twist.explanation: Quiero continuar stacks want + infinitive directly.

desear.etymology_derivation: Climb the English register ladder from 'want' to 'desire' and Spanish desear is waiting.

entrar.context_translation: I want to go in here.
entrar.etymology_derivation: Trade phrasal 'go in' for formal 'enter' → entrar (used with en: entrar en la casa).

terminar.context_translation: I want to finish the work.
terminar.etymology_derivation: English 'terminate' sounds like a robot; Spanish terminar is the everyday word for 'finish'!

preferir.etymology_derivation: Stem-changing e → ie in the boot: prefiero, prefieres, prefiere.

importante.etymology_derivation: Adjectives ending in -e do not change for gender: el punto importante, la idea importante.

diferente.etymology_derivation: Invariable for gender in the singular.

posible.etymology_derivation: Spanish simplifies double ss to single s: posible, imposible.

imposible.etymology_derivation: in- becomes im- before p: imposible.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).
